Another studio tries to fund completion of their game (Windborne) through Early Access release on Steam; announces discontinuation of development. Indie devs beware: the golden age may be over.

There never was a golden age of Early Access in my opinion. There were a small handful of games that successfully managed a release after doing Early Access, but not nearly enough to make it a respectable business model. I personally didn't get burned- but after taking a risk on Minecraft and Kerbal Space Program I realized that anything other than an open world game where you make your own fun just isn't going to be able to handle the Early Access model. I'd be too nervous to take a dive on any new open world games now though. There have simply been too many failures, and too many people have gotten burned.

The golden age of Early Access was before it was called Early Access.

When Minecraft and KSP were doing it because they had pretty sweet games already but wanted to keep adding features, so just said "You can buy it now, but it's not done yet. We're gonna make it even better."

Steam turned it into "Our game hit alpha, give us money now or we won't bother to finish."

That might have been the case for KSP. But Minecraft was a lazy product from start to finish. Notch started asking for money when it was still just a lazy clone of Infiniminer. Development was slow and Notch's blog indicated that he was often too engrossed in playing video games to work on develop it. Rana indicated that they had considering redoing the graphics, which had always simply been placeholders, but decided instead to leave everything as-is. They finally declared Minecraft was out of alpha when it had barely changed from what it was when survival mode first came out. It wasn't finished by any means, it was just popular now and it was time to double the price and cash in.

Honestly, if any early access game is to be praised for being fun from the start and continuing to add features, I'd say it's Terraria. And KSP.

I think the difference is that Steam made it a business model, and a profitable one at that. Minecraft was the first game that I know of that had any real commercial success in Early Release, prior to that nobody even bothered to offer Early Access because nobody payed for it, so you would build a whole distribution channel for all 100 people that would actually pay for it. Steam flipped that on its head. You no longer really had to have a distribution channel because Steam provided it for you. Steam provided the advertising for you. Steam provided payment processing. All of the hurdles it would usually take that made Early Access not worth it are now gone. Now you can just take a build, slap it on Steam, and start charging money. You're entirely right about the state of completion in KSP and Minecraft though. Those games were really closer to a beta, but a beta that kept adding features. I didn't notice a lot of horrendous flaws in either of them, other than occasional glitches or crashes (but then again, that's true of a lot of released games anymore).

Steam has also massively disincentivized actually completing the game. Now it seems like the goal is to get that one big hit, where your game makes it to the front page of Reddit and hordes of people buy it. Previously, Early Access was a good way to get advertising for your game. You give out some keys, people play it, they tell their friends, etc, etc, but you didn't really expect to make much money off the Early Access, that was just to get people excited about the game. Now that a significant chunk of your earnings happen before the game is released, there's a serious decision to make. Do we keep working on the game full steam and hope that the earnings after release will outweigh the costs of finishing the game? Or do we cut down to a skeleton crew that just more or less maintains the game so it keeps running? More and more it seems like people take option 2 because it's safe. You already have your money, why risk it?

Minecraft and KSP also have something else going for it that contributed greatly to their success. They both support and even encourage Mods. The mod community has a very real place in the success of those two games.

One of the things I particularly liked about how KSP did it is that the game was very cheap - <$10, I think - in the beginning. But as the game got more features, they began to charge more. For me, with KSP, it was just a matter of when I thought it would be a game I'd want to play, and that ended up being around the time they added save games and the ability to launch multiple ships/flights at once.

As for Minecraft though, well, I'm really glad someone came up with Tekkit and Forge.
